And I usually think about do is better than show is better than tell, meaning you want to remove all the frictions and somehow give them a warm start, give them some sample template, give them some sample thing they can play with initially in that very moment already, and you can supplement that with your email to bring them to the product if they don't do that. So that's activation. If activation is okay, but your conversion, your self-check checkout flow, usually there are also room for improvement. One company, when I look at their data, they find that India has very low success rate, which is expected, but we begin to say it's because the payment solution they choose actually doesn't support that market well. grounded_result.question: Based on the podcast, give me a three-step plan to improve onboarding for a product with poor activation.

answer.summary: Set a product-specific activation goal, find what is blocking users from reaching it, then redesign and test a guided first-use experience that helps them get value quickly. This three-step plan synthesizes the podcast’s recommendations; it is not a guaranteed result.

sections.heading: 1. Define the activation goal
sections.content: Choose an aha-moment or activation metric that represents users reaching real product value—not just signing up or logging in. Treat it as the goalpost for improving onboarding; the right milestone depends on the product and may reflect team behavior or later retention.

sections.heading: 2. Diagnose why users get stuck
sections.content: Walk through the experience as a new user and use funnel data to identify confusing steps and the biggest drop-offs. Then investigate why users leave: ask users who stall what happened, and combine those answers with the step-by-step data. Prioritize experiments on the largest losses rather than guessing or testing changes without understanding the problem.

sections.heading: 3. Guide users to value, then test and refine
sections.content: Make the first experience help users do something valuable: remove friction, offer a warm start such as a sample template, and guide them through small concrete actions instead of leaving them with a blank page or merely explaining features. Tailor the experience to users’ needs where possible, then run experiments on the high-impact opportunities and measure activation against the goal from step one.

workspace_response.message:
Set a product-specific activation goal, find what is blocking users from reaching it, then redesign and test a guided first-use experience that helps them get value quickly. This three-step plan synthesizes the podcast’s recommendations; it is not a guaranteed result. [S1] [S3] [S10]

## 1. Define the activation goal

Choose an aha-moment or activation metric that represents users reaching real product value—not just signing up or logging in. Treat it as the goalpost for improving onboarding; the right milestone depends on the product and may reflect team behavior or later retention.

[S1] [S5] [S6]

## 2. Diagnose why users get stuck

Walk through the experience as a new user and use funnel data to identify confusing steps and the biggest drop-offs. Then investigate why users leave: ask users who stall what happened, and combine those answers with the step-by-step data. Prioritize experiments on the largest losses rather than guessing or testing changes without understanding the problem.

[S1] [S2] [S3] [S9]

## 3. Guide users to value, then test and refine

Make the first experience help users do something valuable: remove friction, offer a warm start such as a sample template, and guide them through small concrete actions instead of leaving them with a blank page or merely explaining features. Tailor the experience to users’ needs where possible, then run experiments on the high-impact opportunities and measure activation against the goal from step one.

[S1] [S3] [S7] [S8] [S10] [S11]

Why they ignored most of their customer feedback on their way to finding product market fit, and also how you can use his approach to finding product market fit for your own company. Also, the power of game design in building great products, a very contrarian take on pricing strategy, what Rahul has learned about building scaled products on top of AI and LLMs and so much more.

(00:16:53):

Lenny Rachitsky (00:16:54):
Okay, let's get into it. Let's talk about this framework. Maybe just as a broad strokes overview, how does this framework work? How do companies find product-market fit?

Todd Jackson (00:17:03):
So the framework starts with a very simple idea that is product-market fit is not a one-size-fits-all thing, and it doesn't just happen overnight. And for B2B companies, specifically, it does tend to follow a repeatable pattern. And so we start with defining the ultimate goal. The ultimate goal is to get to extreme product-market fit. And we have a precise definition for this. Let me read it to you. So extreme product-market fit is a state of widespread demand for a product that satisfies a critical need and crucially can be delivered repeatably and efficiently to each customer.

(00:17:40):
And so there's three key ideas in there: demand, satisfaction and efficiency. And I think efficiency is worth highlighting because that's what most people would leave out of their definition. You talk about like, "Oh, it's a product, people like it. That's good, that's product-market fit." But if you look, there's products out there. I was a big fan of WeWork, as a customer of WeWork. And I'm a fan of Casper and these other products. Those products managed to achieve customer satisfaction and demand, but they never got the efficiency right, and so the whole business just never worked at scale.

I love it. And it's so interesting that people think of product-market fit, as you said, as this binary, "I have it or I don't." And the way you're talking about this is in this level to developing product-market fit, a company has 25 satisfied customers, they're over five million in ARR, a lot of cases they have 20 employees.

a new product they've never used goes away, that's a high bar. Most people are like, "Ah, whatever. I don't need this thing." And you're saying you look for 50% of people feeling very disappointed if this new thing they've never used before goes away.

So we put a lot of analytical effort, and a lot of depth of thinking. passages.text:
think this is a really cool real case study illustrative example that we can analyze. So let me ask you this, what did you notice that told you something needed to change at Superhuman? And then what did you change that actually had the most impact on your ability to ship and move faster?

Rahul Vohra (00:14:37):
I think what we noticed was this sentiment, and we felt it first ourselves, but we also started hearing it from the market, from our users, from our customers, that we'd slowed down. And as a founder, as a CEO, that's the absolute last thing you want to hear. It's our job after all to speed things up. When I ask people what do they mean by slowing down, they didn't mean the product, of course, the product wasn't working any slower, but that the pace of delivery seemed to have slowed down.

(00:15:09):
I think to break this down, it's important to start by defining what we mean by a slowdown. There's the kind of slowdown that is unavoidable in certain spaces, and then there is the kind of slowdown that is quite avoidable. We actually had both. So starting with unavoidable slowdown, you can classify anything that you build in a company into one of two categories, solution deepening and market widening. Now, solution deepening means making your product better for its existing users, but not making it available to more users. Whereas market widening means making your product available to more users, but not making the product itself any better.

passages.title: Superhuman's secret to success | Rahul Vohra (CEO and founder)
passages.text:
that many people. That's really interesting. Because I always imagined it was like a massive team, but 20 people can handle a lot, is the takeaway there. What was the scale where you stopped manual onboarding, just for folks that are thinking about doing this and then when to stop?

Rahul Vohra (00:48:55):
I think the reason to stop is that there will always be certain personality types who do not want to go through a one-on-one onboarding. At a certain point those people will become very important, and you'll need to be ready with a world-class self-service option. When we started building self-service, it seemed nearly impossible. In fact, it was terrifying, because it's difficult to overstate how much the entire DNA of the company was built around this idea that we would onboard users manually. After all, we did so much in our one-to-one onboardings and there's only so much that software can do. Now, we did after a lot of grind and persistence eventually figure it out and we have a world-class self-service experience today, but we did not at the time.

(00:49:49):
So the flip side is, why would you even do this to begin with? What we found is two things. Number one, the user metrics are excellent for things like engagement, retention, product market fit score, MPS, virality, for all of those metrics. I think you you'll significantly beat your industry benchmarks if you go to the effort of one-on-one onboarding your early customers. It becomes so powerful to have that early cohort of super fans when it comes to things like building a brand. If folks remember that conversation from way up at the top, what is it that creates true virality? It's not viral mechanics, it's word of mouth. It is brand. This is how you can kickstart a brand.

grounded_result.question: What does the 40 percent threshold mean in Rahul Vohra's product-market-fit survey?

answer.summary: The 40% threshold means at least 40% of surveyed users say they’d be “very disappointed” if they could no longer use the product. It’s a useful product-market-fit signal and target, not a guarantee or a rigid cutoff.

sections.heading: What the percentage measures
sections.content: Rahul Vohra describes asking users how they’d feel if they could no longer use the product, with choices including “very disappointed.” The 40% benchmark means that 40% or more of respondents choose that answer. The evidence describing the benchmark comes from Sean Ellis, while Rahul’s excerpt describes the survey question.

sections.heading: How to interpret it
sections.content: Treat 40% as a practical team target for deciding when to pursue growth more aggressively—not a precise or guaranteed dividing line. It’s a leading indicator; continued use and retention are a stronger test. A meaningful sample matters: Ellis says 10 responses is too few to rely on for a go-to-market decision, and he aimed for at least 30 responses.

The 40% threshold means at least 40% of surveyed users say they’d be “very disappointed” if they could no longer use the product. It’s a useful product-market-fit signal and target, not a guarantee or a rigid cutoff. [S1] [S2] [S5] [S6]

## What the percentage measures

Rahul Vohra describes asking users how they’d feel if they could no longer use the product, with choices including “very disappointed.” The 40% benchmark means that 40% or more of respondents choose that answer. The evidence describing the benchmark comes from Sean Ellis, while Rahul’s excerpt describes the survey question.

[S1] [S2]

## How to interpret it

Treat 40% as a practical team target for deciding when to pursue growth more aggressively—not a precise or guaranteed dividing line. It’s a leading indicator; continued use and retention are a stronger test. A meaningful sample matters: Ellis says 10 responses is too few to rely on for a go-to-market decision, and he aimed for at least 30 responses.

grounded_result.question: What is an opportunity solution tree, and how does Teresa Torres use it?

answer.summary: The opportunity solution tree is a visual framework used to structure the opportunity space and solutions. It helps product teams shift from an output focus to an outcome focus. The framework is challenging to apply in practice because it requires teams to differentiate between the problem space and the solution space.

sections.heading: What is an opportunity solution tree?
sections.content: An opportunity solution tree is a visual framework used to structure the opportunity space and solutions. It's a tree visual that starts with an outcome at the root, branches into the opportunity space, and then branches into solutions.

sections.heading: The purpose of the opportunity solution tree
sections.content: The purpose of the opportunity solution tree is to add structure to the complex problem of figuring out what to build by starting from an outcome.

sections.heading: The challenge of structuring the opportunity space
sections.content: The challenge of structuring the opportunity space is that many teams struggle to differentiate between the problem space and the solution space. Most people write opportunities as solutions, and it's hard to teach people to be comfortable with staying in the problem space.

sections.heading: How to apply the opportunity solution tree
sections.content: To apply the opportunity solution tree, teams need to interview customers, collect stories, and structure the opportunity space using an experience map. They need to differentiate between the problem space and the solution space, and make sure to write opportunities in a way that describes the problem.

sections.heading: Challenges of implementing the opportunity solution tree
sections.content: Implementing the opportunity solution tree can be challenging because it requires teams to fundamentally shift their job from being told to build features to figuring out what to build based on customer needs. It also requires teams to develop new skills, such as interviewing customers and framing opportunities.

sections.heading: Using the opportunity solution tree in a growing company
sections.content: As a company grows, the opportunity solution tree remains the same, but the challenges of implementing it may change. In a larger company, teams need to consider adjacent teams and dependencies, and make sure to share their discovery work and be aware of what other teams are working on.

workspace_response.message:
The opportunity solution tree is a visual framework used to structure the opportunity space and solutions. It helps product teams shift from an output focus to an outcome focus. The framework is challenging to apply in practice because it requires teams to differentiate between the problem space and the solution space. [S1] [S6]

## What is an opportunity solution tree?

An opportunity solution tree is a visual framework used to structure the opportunity space and solutions. It's a tree visual that starts with an outcome at the root, branches into the opportunity space, and then branches into solutions.

[S1]

## The purpose of the opportunity solution tree

The purpose of the opportunity solution tree is to add structure to the complex problem of figuring out what to build by starting from an outcome.

[S1]

## The challenge of structuring the opportunity space

The challenge of structuring the opportunity space is that many teams struggle to differentiate between the problem space and the solution space. Most people write opportunities as solutions, and it's hard to teach people to be comfortable with staying in the problem space.

[S6]

## How to apply the opportunity solution tree

To apply the opportunity solution tree, teams need to interview customers, collect stories, and structure the opportunity space using an experience map. They need to differentiate between the problem space and the solution space, and make sure to write opportunities in a way that describes the problem.

[S4] [S5] [S6]

## Challenges of implementing the opportunity solution tree

Implementing the opportunity solution tree can be challenging because it requires teams to fundamentally shift their job from being told to build features to figuring out what to build based on customer needs. It also requires teams to develop new skills, such as interviewing customers and framing opportunities.

[S9]

## Using the opportunity solution tree in a growing company

As a company grows, the opportunity solution tree remains the same, but the challenges of implementing it may change. In a larger company, teams need to consider adjacent teams and dependencies, and make sure to share their discovery work and be aware of what other teams are working on.

[S11]

grounded_result.question: What is an opportunity solution tree, and how does Teresa Torres use it?

answer.summary: Teresa Torres describes the opportunity solution tree as a visual scaffold for moving from a desired outcome to customer opportunities, possible solutions, and sometimes assumption tests. She uses customer stories and an experience map to organize opportunities, then works toward specific, solvable needs before choosing solutions.

sections.heading: What the tree is for
sections.content: It is a decision-tree-like visual: the desired outcome sits at the root, with branches for the opportunity space, then solutions, and potentially assumption tests. Torres created it to give teams structure for the difficult shift from being handed features to figuring out what to build to achieve an outcome. An opportunity is an unmet need, pain point, or desire—not a proposed solution; she says teams often mistakenly write opportunities as solutions.

sections.heading: How Torres applies it
sections.content: She recommends grounding opportunities in customer stories gathered through interviews. Rather than asking only general questions such as what someone likes to watch, ask them to recount a specific recent experience; the details can reveal needs and pain points. Then frame opportunities specifically enough to address—for example, difficulty selecting letters on an Apple TV remote when entering a password or searching for a title—instead of a broad wish like “make it easier to use.” She organizes the opportunity space around a common experience map, and as the tree branches downward, opportunities become smaller and more actionable while still contributing to the larger outcome.

sections.heading: Example: streaming entertainment
sections.content: For an outcome such as getting people to watch more Netflix, Torres maps opportunities to stages in the streaming-entertainment experience: the trigger to watch something, deciding what to watch, and the viewing experience. She gives “I can’t decide what to watch” as a large, ongoing opportunity, which can be broken down into more specific needs—for instance, not knowing whether a show is any good, and wanting to know its cast. She suggests keeping the top-level opportunity branches cognitively manageable, roughly three to seven.

workspace_response.message:
Teresa Torres describes the opportunity solution tree as a visual scaffold for moving from a desired outcome to customer opportunities, possible solutions, and sometimes assumption tests. She uses customer stories and an experience map to organize opportunities, then works toward specific, solvable needs before choosing solutions. [S1] [S3] [S6] [S8]

## What the tree is for

It is a decision-tree-like visual: the desired outcome sits at the root, with branches for the opportunity space, then solutions, and potentially assumption tests. Torres created it to give teams structure for the difficult shift from being handed features to figuring out what to build to achieve an outcome. An opportunity is an unmet need, pain point, or desire—not a proposed solution; she says teams often mistakenly write opportunities as solutions.

[S1] [S2]

## How Torres applies it

She recommends grounding opportunities in customer stories gathered through interviews. Rather than asking only general questions such as what someone likes to watch, ask them to recount a specific recent experience; the details can reveal needs and pain points. Then frame opportunities specifically enough to address—for example, difficulty selecting letters on an Apple TV remote when entering a password or searching for a title—instead of a broad wish like “make it easier to use.” She organizes the opportunity space around a common experience map, and as the tree branches downward, opportunities become smaller and more actionable while still contributing to the larger outcome.

[S7] [S8] [S6] [S9] [S5]

## Example: streaming entertainment

For an outcome such as getting people to watch more Netflix, Torres maps opportunities to stages in the streaming-entertainment experience: the trigger to watch something, deciding what to watch, and the viewing experience. She gives “I can’t decide what to watch” as a large, ongoing opportunity, which can be broken down into more specific needs—for instance, not knowing whether a show is any good, and wanting to know its cast. She suggests keeping the top-level opportunity branches cognitively manageable, roughly three to seven.

[S3] [S4] [S5]

grounded_result.question: What are Richard Rumelt's main components of good strategy?

answer.summary: Rumelt’s strategy kernel has three parts: a diagnosis of the key challenge, a guiding policy for addressing it, and coherent actions that implement the policy.

sections.heading: The three components
sections.content: 1. **Diagnosis:** Explain the situation and identify the important challenge or problem. 2. **Guiding policy:** Set out how you will deal with that challenge. 3. **Coherent actions:** Specify connected actions that put the guiding policy into effect. Rumelt says all three must be present; if any is missing, it is not really a strategy.

sections.heading: What makes the actions strategic
sections.content: Actions should reinforce one another and be few enough to maintain focus—not an expansive list of priorities. As an example, Rumelt describes Microsoft adapting to AI: diagnose the challenge, adopt a policy of investing in a major leader and incorporating the technology into its search engine, then take coherent actions to carry that out.

grounded_result.question: How does April Dunford suggest identifying a product's competitive alternatives?

answer.summary: April Dunford says to identify what a customer would do if your product did not exist: include both the status quo and any alternatives that make the buyer’s shortlist, not just products that look like yours. In B2B, status quo can be manual work or tools like spreadsheets, and “no decision” is a meaningful competitor.

sections.heading: Identify what you must beat
sections.content: Ask, “If we didn’t exist, what would a customer do?” Dunford calls the answers your competitive alternatives. Include two groups: (1) the status quo—the company’s current way of trying to solve the problem, even if it is poor; and (2) the other options that land on the buyer’s shortlist if they decide to purchase something different. Don’t limit the list to products that resemble yours.

sections.heading: Count status quo and indecision
sections.content: Status quo might mean a spreadsheet, pen and paper, interns, or manual labor. Dunford warns against discounting it: she says B2B businesses lose about 40% of deals to “no decision,” which can mean the buyer stays with the existing approach. Her positioning advice is to treat both that status quo and shortlisted alternatives as things you need to beat to win the deal.

workspace_response.message:
April Dunford says to identify what a customer would do if your product did not exist: include both the status quo and any alternatives that make the buyer’s shortlist, not just products that look like yours. In B2B, status quo can be manual work or tools like spreadsheets, and “no decision” is a meaningful competitor. [S1] [S2] [S3]

## Identify what you must beat

Ask, “If we didn’t exist, what would a customer do?” Dunford calls the answers your competitive alternatives. Include two groups: (1) the status quo—the company’s current way of trying to solve the problem, even if it is poor; and (2) the other options that land on the buyer’s shortlist if they decide to purchase something different. Don’t limit the list to products that resemble yours.

[S1] [S2]

## Count status quo and indecision

Status quo might mean a spreadsheet, pen and paper, interns, or manual labor. Dunford warns against discounting it: she says B2B businesses lose about 40% of deals to “no decision,” which can mean the buyer stays with the existing approach. Her positioning advice is to treat both that status quo and shortlisted alternatives as things you need to beat to win the deal.

[S2] [S3]

Ronny Kohavi (00:26:42):
Yeah, a dollar question that everybody asks. So actually, we'll put this in the notes, but I gave a talk last year, what I called it is practical defaults. And one of the things I show there is that unless you have at least tens of thousands of users, the math, the statistics just don't work out for most of the metrics that you're interested in.

Ronny Kohavi (00:27:05):
In fact, I gave an actual practical number of a retail site with some conversion rate, trying to detect changes that are at least 5% beneficial, which is something that startups should focus on. They shouldn't focus on the 1%, they should focus on the 5 and 10%. Then you need something like 200,000 users.

Ronny Kohavi (00:27:25):
So start experimenting when you're in the tens of thousands of users. You'll only be able to detect large effects. And then once you get to 200,000 users, then the magic starts happening. Then you can start testing a lot more. Then you have the ability to test everything and make sure that you're not degrading and getting value out of experimentation. So you ask for rule of thumb, 200,000 users, you're magical. Below that, start building the culture, start building the platform, start integrating. So that as you scale, you start to see the value.

Ronny Kohavi (00:56:00):
If you design the experiment to send 50% of users to control and 50% of users to treatment, it's supposed to be a random number, or a hash function. If you get something off from 50%, it's a red flag.

Ronny Kohavi (00:56:15):
So let's take a real example. Let's say you're running an experiment, and it's large, it's got a million users, and you've got 50.2. So people say, "Well, I don't know. My design was 50/50, and it tells you the probability that this could have happened by chance.

Ronny Kohavi (00:56:45):
Now in a case like this, you plug in the numbers, it might tell you that this should happen one in half a million experiments. Well, unless you've run half a million experiment, very unlikely that you would get a 50.2 versus 49.8 split. And therefore, something is wrong with the experiment.

Ronny Kohavi (00:13:31):
Well, first of all, I published three different numbers for my career. So overall at Microsoft, about 66%, two thirds of ideas fail. And don't think the 66 is accurate. It's about two thirds. At Bing, which is a much more optimized domain after we've been optimizing it for a while, the failure rate was around 85%. Ronny Kohavi (00:14:09):

grounded_result.question: According to Ronny Kohavi, what can make A/B test results misleading?

answer.summary: Kohavi warns that misleading A/B results can come from sample-ratio mismatches, repeatedly checking results and stopping once they look significant, or treating a nominal p-value as the chance a finding is false.

sections.heading: Sample-ratio mismatch
sections.content: If a test designed to split users 50/50 produces a materially different split, that is a red flag: the experiment may be wrong and its results should not be trusted. Kohavi gives the example of a million-user test split 50.2/49.8; a statistical check might show that such a result would occur by chance only about once in half a million experiments. Possible causes include bots interacting with control and treatment at different rates, data-pipeline problems, skewed traffic filtering, or campaigns sending users into an experiment partway through the site. Microsoft found about 8% of experiments had this mismatch.

sections.heading: Repeatedly checking p-values and stopping when significant
sections.content: Using real-time p-value monitoring to stop an experiment as soon as it becomes significant inflates the false-positive (type I error) rate. Kohavi says a nominal 5% error rate could become roughly 30% with this approach.

sections.heading: Misreading statistical significance
sections.content: A p-value is not the probability that the result is false; it is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true. The false-positive risk also depends on the prior likelihood that the tested idea succeeds. For Airbnb search, where the success rate was 8%, Kohavi gives a 26% chance of a false positive even for a statistically significant result with p < 0.05.

this is for and how to think about this. So maybe a first question is just why do you believe people need a framework for finding product-market fit? And just also, if you want to touch on why is product-market fit so important? Why is that something people should even be thinking about?

The thing about product-market fit is that I find it's mysterious to a lot of people, and people tend to think about it purely as an art rather than a science. That was published on the First Round Review in 2018, and it was immediately popular and interesting to people. And I think the reason is because it was specific and because it was tactical and it brought a little bit of the science to something that people thought was just an art. think this is a really cool real case study illustrative example that we can analyze. So let me ask you this, what did you notice that told you something needed to change at Superhuman? And then what did you change that actually had the most impact on your ability to ship and move faster?

Rahul Vohra (00:14:37):
I think what we noticed was this sentiment, and we felt it first ourselves, but we also started hearing it from the market, from our users, from our customers, that we'd slowed down. And as a founder, as a CEO, that's the absolute last thing you want to hear. It's our job after all to speed things up. When I ask people what do they mean by slowing down, they didn't mean the product, of course, the product wasn't working any slower, but that the pace of delivery seemed to have slowed down.

(00:15:09):
I think to break this down, it's important to start by defining what we mean by a slowdown. There's the kind of slowdown that is unavoidable in certain spaces, and then there is the kind of slowdown that is quite avoidable. We actually had both. So starting with unavoidable slowdown, you can classify anything that you build in a company into one of two categories, solution deepening and market widening. Now, solution deepening means making your product better for its existing users, but not making it available to more users. Whereas market widening means making your product available to more users, but not making the product itself any better.

passages.text:
17:45):
I'm glad you got into this, I was going to get into how you measure this stuff. So what it sounds like is the Sean Ellis survey is used as you iterate and launch towards launch. And then NPS is maybe post-launch to see how people like the product.

Jag Duggal (00:18:01):
NPS is post-launch. We also look at metrics like churn to make sure that we're not building a leaky bucket, and that's part of this viral customer acquisition loop that we've built. We want to make sure we're building products that are great enough that our customers will tell their friends, and we don't have to invest as much in marketing to drive our growth. And that only works if the customers you get you retain. I have built earlier in my career products that have leaky buckets, and that's a very frustrating treadmill to be on. So I am personally maniacal about making sure that the bucket doesn't have a hole in the bottom.

Lenny Rachitsky (00:18:42):
So in this Sean Ellis piece, which is really interesting because I think it's something a lot of people can adopt if they're trying to build products people love, and also that succeed. Is this a goal for every project? And I don't know the strategy, or the one pager. Or is it just implied, "Okay, we're not going to move past this gate if 50%, less than 50% of people are not very disappointed." Is that how it's operationalized?

passages.text:
is, think about the features of their product. Do those features indulge, playful, exploration? Are they fun even without a goal? And do they elicit moments of pleasant surprise? If so, you have a toy and you can combine that with other toys and actually start to build a game.

Lenny Rachitsky (01:05:28):
If people were to listen to this segment of the podcast, they would never guess we're talking about B2B software and email, which I love. Let's talk about pricing strategy and your approach to pricing. Another very contrarian approach that you guys took where you charge $30 a month for email that was free, that people don't need to pay for anywhere. And it's worked and now a lot of companies are thinking of it this way. You've even raised your prices recently. What have you learned about pricing strategy that you think might be helpful to folks?

Rahul Vohra (01:05:58):
I always say the same thing when it comes to pricing, which is before you figure out pricing, you must first figure out positioning. Superhuman is the best email tool on the market. We fortunately have the metrics to show this. One of the cool things about selling an email tool, is you can compare the 30 days prior to using Superhuman to the 30 days after, or the year before to the year after. We do that obviously. We're able to show that people get through their email twice as fast with Superhuman, that they respond one to two days faster, and that they save four hours or more every single week. Because of that, we're very confident in saying that Superhuman is the best email tool on the market and that we're building it for high performing teams and high performing individuals. In other words, we serve the high end of the market.

passages.title: A framework for finding product-market fit | Todd Jackson (First Round Capital)
passages.text:
you're going to get for your company, for your product. And if you have product-market fit, and as you are progressing along this journey, the marginal customer should be getting easier and easier and easier to get, easier to acquire them, easier to give them good service with a good product.

(00:19:42):
And that means your efficiency is increasing along the way and your product-market fit is strengthening. So you've got to have all three of those things: demand, satisfaction, efficiency. But the interesting thing is that you don't go for all three of them at once from the very beginning. And so product-market fit, it happens in the sequence of levels, it happens over multiple years. And for the best enterprise companies, I would say they tend to reach extreme product-market fit in roughly four to six years. There's some variance, but roughly four to six years. And so we label these four levels. We say level one product-market fit is nascent product-market fit. Level two is developing, level three is strong, and level four is extreme. And that's where you want to get.

(00:20:26):
And along the way, you're trading off these three dimensions: satisfaction, demand, and efficiency because they're intertwined. You could spend a bunch of money on marketing, and that's going to increase your demand, but you're decreasing your efficiency if you do that. You can invest a bunch in efficiency and automating a whole bunch of stuff, but that actually might harm the customer experience and you're reducing satisfaction. So that's an interesting thing, I think, is you're actually making trade-offs at each level and what you should optimize for at each level is different. And so we talk about all these signs, whether you're getting stuck at a given level, how do you get unstuck and how do you progress along this path.

grounded_result.question: Compare Sean Ellis's and Rahul Vohra's approaches to measuring product-market fit. What do they have in common?

answer.summary: Both use the “how would you feel if you could no longer use this product?” question and treat “very disappointed” responses as evidence of product-market fit. Ellis uses the score to identify must-have users and guide growth; Vohra describes a system for measuring and optimizing fit, including using an algorithm to shape the roadmap.

sections.heading: Sean Ellis’s approach
sections.content: Ellis’s test offers response options including very disappointed, somewhat disappointed, and not disappointed. He looks for the people who would be very disappointed—the product’s must-have users—and uses their feedback to understand who they are, what benefit they value, and how they use the product. He recommends focusing the roadmap and related work, such as onboarding and messaging, on serving those users, rather than acting on somewhat-disappointed users’ feedback. He describes 40% as a useful target for aligning a team on when to grow, not a firm 39%-versus-41% cutoff. The test is a leading indicator; retention and actual product use are the ultimate test.

sections.heading: Rahul Vohra’s approach
sections.content: Vohra also measures fit by asking how people would feel if they could no longer use the product, with “very disappointed” as one of the responses. He says fit can be measured, optimized, and increased systematically, and that an algorithm can write a roadmap intended to increase it. He also stresses listening intensely while deliberately not acting on feedback from many early users: the product cannot be for everybody. The supplied passages do not specify a numeric threshold for Vohra’s method or the detailed mechanics of his algorithm.

sections.heading: What they have in common
sections.content: Both use the same core question and response concept to make product-market fit measurable, rather than relying only on intuition. Both connect measurement to action: the goal is to learn what people value and improve the product for the users it serves. Their shared focus is not on satisfying every user; Ellis centers must-have users, while Vohra cautions against acting on feedback from many early users.

workspace_response.message:
Both use the “how would you feel if you could no longer use this product?” question and treat “very disappointed” responses as evidence of product-market fit. Ellis uses the score to identify must-have users and guide growth; Vohra describes a system for measuring and optimizing fit, including using an algorithm to shape the roadmap. [S1] [S2] [S4] [S6] [S7]

## Sean Ellis’s approach

Ellis’s test offers response options including very disappointed, somewhat disappointed, and not disappointed. He looks for the people who would be very disappointed—the product’s must-have users—and uses their feedback to understand who they are, what benefit they value, and how they use the product. He recommends focusing the roadmap and related work, such as onboarding and messaging, on serving those users, rather than acting on somewhat-disappointed users’ feedback. He describes 40% as a useful target for aligning a team on when to grow, not a firm 39%-versus-41% cutoff. The test is a leading indicator; retention and actual product use are the ultimate test.

[S1] [S3] [S6] [S7] [S8] [S11]

## Rahul Vohra’s approach

Vohra also measures fit by asking how people would feel if they could no longer use the product, with “very disappointed” as one of the responses. He says fit can be measured, optimized, and increased systematically, and that an algorithm can write a roadmap intended to increase it. He also stresses listening intensely while deliberately not acting on feedback from many early users: the product cannot be for everybody. The supplied passages do not specify a numeric threshold for Vohra’s method or the detailed mechanics of his algorithm.

[S2] [S4] [S5]

## What they have in common

Both use the same core question and response concept to make product-market fit measurable, rather than relying only on intuition. Both connect measurement to action: the goal is to learn what people value and improve the product for the users it serves. Their shared focus is not on satisfying every user; Ellis centers must-have users, while Vohra cautions against acting on feedback from many early users.

And so I basically got involved in every single detail and I basically told leaders that leaders are in the details. And there's this negative term called micromanagement. I think there's a difference between micromanagement, which is like telling people exactly what to do, and being in the details. Being in the details is what every responsible company's board does to the CEO. That doesn't mean the board is telling them what to do. But if you don't know the details, how do you know people are doing a good job? People think that great leader's job is to hire people and just empower them to do a good job. answer.summary: Brian Chesky said he did not fire every product manager. He made the product-management group smaller and changed how teams worked, including moving many PMs into program-management roles and taking a more direct role in product reviews.

sections.heading: He did not fire every product manager
sections.content: Chesky clarified that he had not gotten rid of the people; his point was about changing how people worked together. He said he made the group much smaller and reassigned many product managers as program managers, training many of them for those roles.

sections.heading: Why he changed the model
sections.content: Chesky described a pattern in which, as he became less involved, projects had more spin, less-clear goals, weaker advocacy, fewer resources, and moved more slowly. He said he later got back into the details and reviewed product and marketing work on a regular cadence. The evidence supports a shift in the operating model—not a mass firing—as his response.

And for the best enterprise companies, I would say they tend to reach extreme product-market fit in roughly four to six years. There's some variance, but roughly four to six years. And so we label these four levels. We say level one product-market fit is nascent product-market fit. Level two is developing, level three is strong, and level four is extreme. And that's where you want to get.

(00:20:26):
And along the way, you're trading off these three dimensions: satisfaction, demand, and efficiency because they're intertwined. You could spend a bunch of money on marketing, and that's going to increase your demand, but you're decreasing your efficiency if you do that. You can invest a bunch in efficiency and automating a whole bunch of stuff, but that actually might harm the customer experience and you're reducing satisfaction. So that's an interesting thing, I think, is you're actually making trade-offs at each level and what you should optimize for at each level is different. And so we talk about all these signs, whether you're getting stuck at a given level, how do you get unstuck and how do you progress along this path.

passages.title: Superhuman's secret to success | Rahul Vohra (CEO and founder)
passages.text:
"How would you feel if you can no longer use this product?" You give them three responses. One of them is very disappointed, the other is somewhat disappointed, and the other is not disappointed. Very disappointed means, "I'd be devastated. I love this product. I need this product."

(00:55:30):
What Sean Ellis found, Sean Ellis, if you don't know him, is the guy who coined the term growth hacker, and he instrumented, benchmarked this initial question. What he found, is that the companies that struggled to grow almost always had less than 40%, very disappointed. Whereas the companies that grew the fastest almost always had more than 40%, very disappointed. And this question, this metric is way more predictive of success than something, for example, like net promoter score.

(00:56:03):
Okay, so far so easy. How do we make this number go up? Well, you want more people to be very disappointed without your product. The trick here is not to act too much on the feedback that the very disappointed people are giving you, because they already love your product. Also, not to act at all really on the feedback that the not disappointed people are giving, you because they're so far from loving your product that they're essentially a lost cause. But to focus on the segment of the somewhat disappointed people, they kind of love your product, but something, and I would wager something small, is holding them back.

that post. I think it is still the most widely shared post on First Round Review, it's called How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product Market Fit, or just Google the Superhuman Product Market Fit Engine. And you'll see the algorithm laid out there fully explained and why it works.

would be like measure your product market fit the way you would for a normal company. So yeah, it's a bit of an art more than the science, but I like the classic if we were to take this product away, what percentage of users would be significantly disappointed or have no other solution?

(00:16:53):
That's right.

Lenny Rachitsky (00:16:54):
Okay, let's get into it. Let's talk about this framework. Maybe just as a broad strokes overview, how does this framework work? How do companies find product-market fit?

Todd Jackson (00:17:03):
So the framework starts with a very simple idea that is product-market fit is not a one-size-fits-all thing, and it doesn't just happen overnight. And for B2B companies, specifically, it does tend to follow a repeatable pattern. And so we start with defining the ultimate goal. The ultimate goal is to get to extreme product-market fit. And we have a precise definition for this. Let me read it to you. So extreme product-market fit is a state of widespread demand for a product that satisfies a critical need and crucially can be delivered repeatably and efficiently to each customer.

(00:17:40):
And so there's three key ideas in there: demand, satisfaction and efficiency. And I think efficiency is worth highlighting because that's what most people would leave out of their definition. You talk about like, "Oh, it's a product, people like it. That's good, that's product-market fit." But if you look, there's products out there. I was a big fan of WeWork, as a customer of WeWork. And I'm a fan of Casper and these other products. Those products managed to achieve customer satisfaction and demand, but they never got the efficiency right, and so the whole business just never worked at scale.

passages.title: A framework for finding product-market fit | Todd Jackson (First Round Capital)
passages.text:
you're going to get for your company, for your product. And if you have product-market fit, and as you are progressing along this journey, the marginal customer should be getting easier and easier and easier to get, easier to acquire them, easier to give them good service with a good product.

(00:19:42):
And that means your efficiency is increasing along the way and your product-market fit is strengthening. So you've got to have all three of those things: demand, satisfaction, efficiency. But the interesting thing is that you don't go for all three of them at once from the very beginning. And so product-market fit, it happens in the sequence of levels, it happens over multiple years. And for the best enterprise companies, I would say they tend to reach extreme product-market fit in roughly four to six years. There's some variance, but roughly four to six years. And so we label these four levels. We say level one product-market fit is nascent product-market fit. Level two is developing, level three is strong, and level four is extreme. And that's where you want to get.

(00:20:26):
And along the way, you're trading off these three dimensions: satisfaction, demand, and efficiency because they're intertwined. You could spend a bunch of money on marketing, and that's going to increase your demand, but you're decreasing your efficiency if you do that. You can invest a bunch in efficiency and automating a whole bunch of stuff, but that actually might harm the customer experience and you're reducing satisfaction. So that's an interesting thing, I think, is you're actually making trade-offs at each level and what you should optimize for at each level is different. And so we talk about all these signs, whether you're getting stuck at a given level, how do you get unstuck and how do you progress along this path.

be enterprise founders, and you ask them, "What did you do in the first six to nine months of running your company, of starting your company? What patterns emerged from that?" And we have found a very consistent set of patterns, and that's what we decided to base our framework around.

Lenny (00:19:08):
Let me follow on that thread real quick because I find some founders still want to have someone come help them with growth even though they know they don't have product market fit, even though this tip comes up every single time when I'm talking to growth person, like, "Wait till you have product market fit before doing growth stuff." Luc Levesque (00:19:27):
Growth advice is generally always applicable. And if you can start thinking about how to build your product early, even if it's pre-product market fit, you're not going to do any damage, but you may be wasting some capital on an advisor or a growth person too early. The problem that I see is if you start growing a product that doesn't have product market fit, you're actually doing more damage than good because you have a product that is now being exposed to the market through growth levers and through optimization that is giving a bad experience with your product. answer.summary: Rahul Vohra’s survey asks users how disappointed they’d be if they could no longer use the product; he uses the share who are “very disappointed” as a product-market-fit signal and recommends focusing improvement work on somewhat-disappointed users. The evidence does not provide tomorrow’s exact Mumbai weather.

sections.heading: Rahul Vohra’s product-market-fit survey
sections.content: Ask users, “How would you feel if you can no longer use this product?” Offer three responses: very disappointed, somewhat disappointed, or not disappointed. “Very disappointed” means they’d be devastated to lose it. Vohra says Sean Ellis found that companies struggling to grow almost always had fewer than 40% very-disappointed users, while the fastest-growing companies almost always had more than 40%; he says this measure is more predictive of success than net promoter score. To improve the result, focus on somewhat-disappointed users: they may already like the product but have something small holding them back. Don’t overreact to feedback from very-disappointed users, who already love it, or focus on not-disappointed users, whom he describes as too far from loving it. Vohra also cautions that product feedback should not be treated as a mandate to satisfy every early user.

S1.title: Superhuman's secret to success | Rahul Vohra (CEO and founder)
S1.text:
"How would you feel if you can no longer use this product?" You give them three responses. One of them is very disappointed, the other is somewhat disappointed, and the other is not disappointed. Very disappointed means, "I'd be devastated. I love this product. I need this product."

(00:55:30):
What Sean Ellis found, Sean Ellis, if you don't know him, is the guy who coined the term growth hacker, and he instrumented, benchmarked this initial question. What he found, is that the companies that struggled to grow almost always had less than 40%, very disappointed. Whereas the companies that grew the fastest almost always had more than 40%, very disappointed. And this question, this metric is way more predictive of success than something, for example, like net promoter score.

(00:56:03):
Okay, so far so easy. How do we make this number go up? Well, you want more people to be very disappointed without your product. The trick here is not to act too much on the feedback that the very disappointed people are giving you, because they already love your product. Also, not to act at all really on the feedback that the not disappointed people are giving, you because they're so far from loving your product that they're essentially a lost cause. But to focus on the segment of the somewhat disappointed people, they kind of love your product, but something, and I would wager something small, is holding them back.

Don’t overreact to feedback from very-disappointed users, who already love it, or focus on not-disappointed users, whom he describes as too far from loving it. Vohra also cautions that product feedback should not be treated as a mandate to satisfy every early user.

Intuition comes not from arbitrariness, it comes from understanding. I would make sure that you have engineering and design ideally report to the founder, product led person. this is not just bad for design, it's bad for product managers and engineers because we all want to build the best products. And one day you wake up and a variety of phenomenon might have happened. And if people are watching this from a large company, here might be some of the characteristics.

The first thing you notice is that these different groups might be running on slightly different technical stacks. That's the first problem. And they may actually be accumulating technical debt. The next problem you'll see is that there's a lot of dependencies. So five teams are going different directions, but they all need a payment platform. And so what happens is that the teams that everyone's dependent on get this backup like a deli and people are going around the block. And then at some point they just give up. So then the teams that are dependent on other people say, "Give me the resources and I'll build this group myself." So instead of five teams going to marketing to get a campaign or to leverage some service, they start building their own marketing departments, their own groups. So now they're really becoming separate divisions. And this is where a division comes from.

passages.title: Brian Chesky’s new playbook
passages.text:
ually started off boarding some responsibilities to program management. The last thing we did is we made the group smaller and more senior. So we don't really have a lot of junior product marketers. So the most senior people are called product marketers, but everyone has to understand how to talk about the product.

(00:07:42):
So the basic idea is this. You can't build a product unless you know how to talk about the product. You can't be an expert in making the product unless you're also an expert in the market of it. And a lot of companies, what they do is they ship a product, it doesn't work, and they say, "We tried that. It didn't work." And if you say you tried and it didn't work, my question is, was it a bad product, a bad strategy or bad execution? Maybe it was a really well-made product, but you had no distribution plan. You had no way to talk about the product. If you build a great product and no one knows about it, did you even build a product? So that is essentially what we do. We have a much smaller function. The people are much more senior. They have much more responsibility. The other thing though is that they do not control or drive designing or engineering. We are a fairly purely functional model. They manage by influence. They do not have control.
